title: Mg: Retool HDD read-head fabs as MgO tunnel-junction memory foundries
idea: HDD head fabs already sputter and pattern CoFeB/MgO tunnel junctions below 30 nm; as hard-drive unit volumes fall, convert these lines to STT-MRAM back-end processing on foundry-supplied CMOS wafers.
why: Adds non-volatile 10-30 ns memory capacity using existing tools and staff, avoiding a ~$10B greenfield fab.

title: Stranded-memory buyback: telemetry finds surplus DIMMs in enterprises
idea: Months-long observation: an agent records each enterprise server's 90-day peak working set, and a buyback service pulls DIMMs above the 99th-percentile need and resells them to cloud and AI buyers.
why: Enterprises typically overprovision RAM by 30-50%. Releasing it is new usable supply at near-zero cost, with no fab and no gases.

title: Memory-footprint labels and app-store fees on bloated software
idea: Worse: let apps ship duplicate runtimes and 2-3x bloat because RAM is treated as free. Flip: app stores, browsers and cloud marketplaces publish a measured resident-memory score per app and apply ranking penalties or listing fees above a category baseline, feeding a memory-efficiency bounty pool.
why: Demand-side supply: trimming client and server footprints 15-30% is worth that much new capacity at zero fab capital.

title: Monolayer molecular doping instead of ion implanters
idea: Scale jump from beamline accelerator to molecule: self-assembled monolayers of phosphorus- or boron-bearing molecules coat the silicon, and a spike anneal drives the dopant in, replacing implanters and their Ar/Xe flood guns for shallow source/drain and periphery junctions.
why: Implanters are high-capex and rare-gas-dependent. Molecular doping is a wet bench process at ~1/10 the capex, with sharper junctions for periphery transistors.

title: Run array litho on non-ASML scanners with relaxed overlay
idea: Inverts 'array lithography needs the tightest overlay from one supplier': print array layers on Nikon/Canon-class immersion scanners with looser overlay, accepting misalignment-induced contact faults in up to 1% of cells.
why: Single-supplier risk and capex: opens a second toolchain at lower cost per scanner.

title: Capacity cascade moving legacy DRAM to depreciated DUV fabs
idea: Po: the oldest fab cures the newest shortage. Auto, industrial and set-top demand for DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 is contractually migrated to fully depreciated 25-38 nm ArF fabs (including revived shuttered lines) under swap agreements: the advanced-node maker gets the freed wafer starts, the old-fab operator gets long-term qualified volume.
why: Legacy grades still occupy a meaningful share of advanced wafers; freeing them for DDR5/HBM adds capacity with no new EUV tools, and depreciated fabs sell bits near cash cost; attacks capital intensity.

title: Whisky-warehouse thermal seasoning during inventory dwell
idea: Like whisky aging in a warehouse while it waits to be sold, wafers and die already held in buffer inventory sit in 150 C bake chambers that double as burn-in, so weak retention cells reveal themselves and are mapped out before packaging; parts ship pre-screened for 10 years at 125 C.
why: Converts idle inventory time into free HTOL screening, raising yield of 125 C-grade parts and removing a separate burn-in step from the supply chain.

title: Active probe-card BIST tiles to break the DRAM test bottleneck
idea: Ideal: testing that is instant and free. Closest achievable at trailing nodes: a 65 nm active probe wafer with one BIST engine per die site tests and burns in every die on the wafer in parallel at speed, cutting reliance on scarce memory ATE.
why: Test and burn-in throughput (especially HBM) 5-10x higher, so finished bits stop waiting in test queues.

title: Shale DUC wells: front-end-complete U.S. wafer bank for surges
idea: Adapted from drilled-but-uncompleted shale wells that wait for prices to rise before fracking: U.S. fabs park wafers in nitrogen stockers once the array and capacitor are done but before final metal and personalization, then finish them in ~3-4 weeks when prices spike.
why: Supply responds ~4x faster than a ~4-month full cycle, and one inventory can serve DDR or LPDDR personalizations, damping price spikes (supply, capital efficiency).

title: Die bank: hold wafers before metal, finish to demand in weeks
idea: Ideal: memory made instantly on order. Closest achievable on existing lines: fabs park WIP wafers in nitrogen stockers at the pre-BEOL hold point (~70% done), then metallize, fuse and package into whichever product is short.
why: Pig cycle and mix mismatch: response time falls from ~4 months to ~4 weeks at low carrying cost.

title: Magnetosome chains: bacteria grow uniform nanomagnets for memory arrays
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria grow chains of uniform 40-50 nm magnetite crystals. Harvested magnetosomes, whose protein shells direct self-assembly onto patterned CMOS, serve as storage bits read by magnetoresistive or Hall sensors; they are grown in fermenters instead of deposited with Pt/Ir/Ru sputter stacks.
why: Swaps scarce precious-metal stacks and fine patterning for fermentation; non-volatile, no capacitor.

title: Crucible-free Czochralski: pull 300 mm ingots from an induction cold-skull
idea: A crucible's only job is to contain molten silicon without contaminating it; a water-cooled segmented copper crucible with induction heating freezes a silicon skull that contains the melt in silicon itself. Adapt cold-crucible melting (used for Ti and nuclear glass) with magnetic melt stirring to CZ pulling, eliminating the high-purity quartz crucible.
why: Scarce resource: removes dependence on Spruce Pine (>80% of HPQ crucible quartz) and lowers interstitial oxygen; the risk is thermal-gradient control at 300 mm diameter.

title: Magnify tiers 300x: convert idle 3D NAND fabs to gain-cell lines
idea: Reuse 3D NAND tool sets (alternating film stacks, one deep channel-hole etch, staircase contacts) to build 300-500 tier vertical-channel IGZO 2T0C gain cells, with a string-select scheme giving random access per tier and aggressive refresh.
why: NAND reached ~$0.05/GB through deposition-defined stacking instead of lithography; borrowing its fab economics targets ~$0.1/GB DRAM-class memory (~100x), trading latency (~100 ns+) and refresh energy, while monetizing underused NAND capacity.

title: Bottle-deposit grandmother: refundable deposit on every memory module
idea: Like a bottle deposit, add a refundable $2-5/GB deposit when DIMMs and LPDDR boards are sold, paid back when the module is returned to a certified refurbisher. This guarantees a steady reverse-logistics flow for harvesting and reuse.
why: Reuse supply: bottle deposits reach 80-90% return rates; capturing retired DRAM systematically could add several % to annual bit supply.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM modules that never dice, test or package dies
idea: Worse: dice every wafer, throw out flawed dies and package survivors one by one. Flip: keep the 300 mm wafer whole as one memory module with defect-tolerant routing and spare-block remapping, bonded directly to a cold-plate carrier board.
why: Eliminates dicing, packaging and known-good-die loss so nearly all good area is used; cost per bit down perhaps 15-25%.

title: Cicada-cycle capacity bank investing only in price troughs
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime-numbered cycles so predators cannot synchronize with them. A public-private capacity bank buys tools and builds shells when DRAM prices crash and incumbents cut capex, then leases the capacity to operators when prices rise.
why: Breaks the boom-bust cycle behind 4x spikes; trough-priced tools cost ~20-30% less.

title: SRAM-only inference fleets bought on logic-foundry capacity
idea: Worse: tie every AI accelerator to HBM supply. Flip: buy inference fleets of SRAM-only chips that shard whole models across hundreds of chips' on-die SRAM, procuring logic-foundry wafers instead of DRAM wafers.
why: Zero refresh, and inference no longer depends on DRAM/HBM supply.

title: Half-inch Minimal Fab lines making legacy DDR3/DDR4 for industrial buyers
idea: Scale jump down from 300 mm wafers to 12.5 mm wafers: desktop tools that each carry their own local clean environment make 40-50 nm-class DRAM for industrial, automotive and defense parts that are being end-of-lifed, with no cleanroom building at all.
why: Leading-edge fabs drop legacy DRAM to chase HBM. A micro-fab costing ~$50M instead of $15B can fill that niche near the customer, which frees big-fab wafers and adds U.S. supply.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM: RDL-stitched good dies on mature wafers
idea: Ideal: memory with no package, socket or dicing. Closest achievable with no new fab: existing OSAT redistribution-layer lines stitch every good die on a mature 2x-nm DRAM wafer into one wafer-scale slab with spare routing around bad dies; one wafer gives ~2 TB on a cold plate serving a rack over CXL.
why: Removes packaging, substrate and final-test cost (~20-30% of module cost) using only existing lines.

title: Substitute declining HDD head fabs for low-temperature memory foundries
idea: Swap the shrinking market for hard-disk read/write heads by converting those thin-film wafer fabs, which already run fine-litho magnetic and oxide processes kept below ~300 C (e.g., in Minnesota), to make BEOL memory tiers.
why: Repurposes existing U.S. cleanrooms, tools and workforce skilled in low-temperature thin films, giving domestic capacity years faster than greenfield.

title: Relabel scandal fixed: certified, graded reclaimed DRAM chips
idea: Harvested DRAM from e-waste got a bad name because chips were sanded, remarked and sold as new. Fix: a certified reclamation line desolders and reballs each chip, runs full retention, speed and row-hammer characterization, writes a tamper-evident provenance record (original lot ID read from the die's fuses plus test results), and sells the chips openly in graded tiers with warranty.
why: Supply: turns millions of discarded DIMMs into trusted bits at a fraction of new cost; recovering even ~5% of annual bit demand matters when prices are 4x.

title: Take-or-pay capacity prepay notes modeled on LNG contracts
idea: Combine 20-year LNG take-or-pay contract structures with fab project finance. Hyperscalers and OEMs sign bit-delivery contracts with floor and ceiling pricing that become bankable collateral for non-recourse debt on a new fab, the way LNG trains are financed.
why: Attacks capital intensity and cyclicality, the reason fabs aren't built until shortages hit. It could lower cost of capital by 3-5 points on $15B+ fabs.

title: Utility-style long-tenor bonds backed by 10-year auto contracts
idea: Like regulated utilities financing dams with 30-year bonds, a fab dedicated to 125 C-qualified memory signs 10-year take-or-pay contracts with automakers and securitizes them into investment-grade bonds at ~5% instead of ~15% equity.
why: Long-life parts create long-life contracts; a 10-point drop in cost of capital cuts wafer cost ~20% since depreciation and financing dominate.

title: Fair-Market-Value Floor Revived: Offtake Price Corridor for New DRAM Fabs
idea: Revive the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement's fair-market-value price floors as a 10-year price corridor: hyperscalers and the government sign take-or-pay contracts with new-entrant fabs at a floor and a cap per Gb, and a stabilization fund pays the difference during gluts and is refilled during spikes.
why: Capital intensity: the bust half of the cycle is what kills new fabs; a floor cuts the cost of capital by several points and makes a $15B fab bankable.

title: Short mean-free-path molybdenum wordlines from U.S. mines replace tungsten
idea: Below ~15 nm width, line resistivity is dominated by electron mean-free-path scattering, where barrier-less Mo (~11 nm MFP) beats W plus TiN liner. Convert buried wordlines and contacts to Mo CVD, tied to offtake contracts with U.S. molybdenum producers (primary and copper by-product).
why: Removes exposure to China's ~80% tungsten share and cuts narrow-line resistance ~20-30%, allowing thinner wordlines.

title: Hyperscaler take-or-pay prepayments bankroll an independent DRAM entrant
idea: Ideal: a fab that costs its builder nothing. Closest achievable: 4-6 hyperscalers prepay 30-40% of a $15B fab as 10-year take-or-pay wafer-start contracts with step-in rights, which makes the rest project-financeable like an LNG terminal.
why: Capital intensity: entrant equity need falls ~60%, adding a fourth independent supplier that buyers have a stake in.

title: Papermaking nanosheets: Langmuir-Blodgett perovskite films with k near 200
idea: Paper forms by settling fibers out of a slurry. Exfoliate layered perovskites (Ca2Nb3O10, Sr2Nb3O10) into 1.5 nm nanosheets in solution and tile them onto wafers layer by layer by Langmuir-Blodgett transfer. This builds capacitor dielectrics with k ~100-200 at near-room temperature.
why: Charge wall needs k~70: ~3x ZrO2's k lets short, cheap capacitors hold 5 fF, with the dielectric made in beakers and no ALD precursor supply chain.

title: Substitute furnace polysilicon with excimer-laser LTPS periphery tiers
idea: Swap furnace-crystallized silicon for display-industry excimer-laser annealing that melts a-Si into high-mobility polysilicon in nanoseconds while the substrate stays below 400 C, giving fast periphery transistors in upper tiers.
why: Reuses the display ELA supply chain, gives ~100 cm^2/Vs periphery transistors in BEOL and enables multi-tier memories with local decoders.

title: Pre-permitted fab-ready federal sites cut construction interest by a third
idea: Time is capital: on a $15B fab every year of construction costs ~$1B in interest and lost output. Pre-certify federal sites with completed environmental review, water recycling, 500 MW interconnects and gas lines so a fab can break ground in weeks and run in ~24 months.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-supply: shaves 1-2 years off the 3-5 year lead time and ~30% of interest during construction.

title: Mandatory RAM-footprint efficiency labels for operating systems and apps
idea: Inverts 'software memory demand is a given': an Energy-Star-style rating (resident memory per standardized task) required for government procurement and shown in app stores, plus OEM incentives to ship with less installed RAM.
why: Demand side: a 20% cut in DRAM per phone and PC across ~1.5B units/yr frees an estimated several percent of world bit supply for servers.

title: Minimal Fab half-inch wafers plus maskless direct-write lithography
idea: Combine Japan's Minimal Fab (0.5-inch wafers, desk-sized local-cleanroom tools) with multibeam e-beam or laser direct-write. The result is a mask-free micro-fab that makes small lots of radiation-hard or specialty DRAM inside defense or auto plants.
why: Cuts capital per site from billions to about $10-30M and removes masks, for secure, distributed niche supply that frees the big fabs for commodity bits.

title: Personality-fused universal die serving DDR, LPDDR or HBM markets
idea: Worse: commit wafers to one interface months before knowing which market will be short. Flip: design one core die carrying DDR5, LPDDR5X and HBM-attach I/O and set its personality by e-fuse at final test, routing finished wafers to whichever market is tightest.
why: Cuts allocation lag and inventory mismatch; shortages shorten and effective supply rises a few percent.

title: Hafnium-free periphery transistors with zirconium-silicate gate dielectrics
idea: DRAM periphery needs EOT ~1.2-1.5 nm, not logic's ~0.8 nm, so HfO2's k~25 is overkill: ZrSiOx (k~12-18) or ZrO2/SiON with TiN gates meets the leakage spec. Qualify a Hf-free periphery high-k metal-gate module fed from widely mined zircon (ZrSiO4).
why: Scarce resource: removes Hf, a by-product with very few refiners, from the periphery at minor performance cost.

title: ESCO shared-savings contracts for reclaiming cold DRAM pages
idea: Like energy-service companies paid from a client's utility savings, a vendor installs a page-temperature profiler and transparent tiering agent that moves cold pages to compressed or CXL far memory, and is paid a fixed share of the DRAM purchases the customer avoids.
why: Typical enterprise servers keep 30-50% cold pages; zero-upfront contracts make adoption fast, cutting new DRAM buying by 20-30%.

title: Negabyte rebates that pay software to shrink memory footprint
idea: Po: memory is negative. Like utility negawatt programs, cloud providers and governments pay software vendors a rebate per GB-hour of verified footprint reduction (fleet telemetry against a baseline), funded by avoided DRAM purchases.
why: Software bloat is the cheapest supply source: 10-30% footprint cuts in ubiquitous runtimes (JVMs, browsers, databases) free capacity worth several fabs' output; attacks cost per usable bit.

title: Debond-on-demand packaging designed for multiple die lives
idea: Like smartphone battery stretch-release adhesives and cradle-to-cradle furniture, package memory in an encapsulant that stays stable for 10 years at 150 C but debonds cleanly at 260 C under a chemical trigger, so die can be recovered intact and repackaged at end of product life.
why: Makes every high-temperature memory die harvestable for 2-3 lives, multiplying effective supply per wafer over decades.

title: Second-source HBM core dies on a standard foundry base die
idea: Box[Source=core dies from smaller DRAM makers x Integration=HBM4 stack on a JEDEC-compliant foundry base die x Owner=base-die vendor as integrator x Finance=multi-sourced KGD contracts]: a neutral integrator buys core-die wafers from second-tier DRAM fabs and stacks them on its own HBM4 base die, delivering standard HBM to GPU makers.
why: Breaks the three-supplier HBM bottleneck: adds second-tier DRAM capacity to HBM supply without changing the HBM interface.

title: Blood bank: type-matched inference-grade DRAM from ECC-failing die
idea: Random stimulus 'blood bank' -> type-match donors to recipients. Die with raw BER of 1e-9 to 1e-6 (rejected today) are typed and sold as 'inference grade' for quantized weights and KV caches, with the controller placing sensitive metadata in the die's strong rows and bulk tensors in weak rows.
why: Turns yield loss into supply: est. +3-6% sellable bits/wafer, cost per usable bit down proportionally, for workloads that already tolerate approximate data.

title: Minify crucible dependence: kerfless epitaxial wafers peeled from templates
idea: Grow 300 mm device-grade silicon by fast epitaxy on a porous-silicon release layer over a reusable template, peel it off, and reuse the template 50x+ with no Czochralski ingot, quartz crucible or wire saw.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and ingot-pulling chokepoints, halves kerf silicon waste, and enables domestic wafer supply.

title: Eliminate one-ingot-per-wafer: reusable donor wafers via porous-silicon transfer
idea: Eliminate consuming a full prime wafer per lot: grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a donor, bond it to lower-grade handle wafers, cleave, and reuse each donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts prime polysilicon, crucible and ingot demand ~5-10x per wafer start; DRAM arrays need only the top tens of microns of perfect silicon.

title: Thin films: porous-silicon release layer enables 10x substrate reuse
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells/thin films: one added mask defines anodization windows that form a buried porous-Si cleave plane; after array processing the thin device layer is bonded to a cheap carrier and lifted off, and the CZ wafer is re-polished and reused ~10 times.
why: Scarce resources: cuts prime-wafer and HPQ crucible demand per bit sharply.

title: Solar-style layer-transfer wafer reuse to escape quartz crucibles
idea: Borrowing kerfless solar and III-V epitaxial lift-off, grow a thick device-grade epi layer on a porous-silicon release layer over a parent CZ wafer, build the DRAM in the epi, bond to a cheap carrier, and lift off, reusing the parent wafer 10-20 times.
why: Cuts demand for CZ ingots and Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucibles by ~90% per bit; a concentrated chokepoint becomes a minor input.

title: Crucible-light wafers by reusable porous-silicon layer transfer
idea: Inverts 'every DRAM wafer is a slice of its own crucible-grown ingot': grow 30-50 um device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer atop a reusable parent wafer, bond it to a cheap carrier, and reuse the parent 30-50 times.
why: Scarce resource: cuts high-purity quartz crucible dependence (Spruce Pine >80%) by ~30x per wafer and lowers substrate cost.

title: Eliminate the package: decap scrap modules, rebond known-good DRAM die
idea: Eliminate the package as a one-way trip: laser plus fuming-acid decapsulation strips mold compound from scrapped DRAM packages, freed dies are re-probed on wafer-sort-style chucks, re-bumped, and re-assembled into new multi-die packages or chiplet substrates.
why: Recovers bits whose EUV/capex cost is already sunk (die is ~85% of module cost); even partial recovery of e-waste DRAM adds a few percent of annual bit supply at low capital.

title: Alien asks why three companies own memory: open DRAM PDK
idea: An alien surveying Earth finds a three-vendor oligopoly. The U.S. buys a full mature-node DRAM process (or requires one through CHIPS conditions): 1y-nm 8 Gb cell, sense amp, redundancy and test flow. It publishes this as a licensed open PDK with a reference die, so any foundry (GF, Intel, SkyWater, TI) can run DRAM wafers on spare 300 mm capacity.
why: U.S. manufacturability and the know-how chokepoint: existing logic foundries could add DRAM output in ~2 years instead of 5; 20k wafers/month adds ~3-4% to world supply.

title: LPDDR5X dies redeployed into DDR5 RDIMMs behind a bridge buffer
idea: Box[Source=LPDDR5X die oversupply from phones x Transform=bridge buffer translating DDR5 protocol to LPDDR x Integration=standard DDR5 RDIMM form factor x Owner=module maker]: when phone demand softens, route mobile die into server RDIMMs where a buffer chip presents a JEDEC DDR5 interface to the host.
why: Supply fungibility across die families; lets mobile capacity cover server shortfalls; host interface unchanged.

title: Second-life CXL memory bricks from retired server DIMM dies
idea: Box[Source=retired DIMMs x Transform=laser debond+KGD retest x Integration=CXL Type-3 x Owner=recycler-OEM JV x Finance=EPR take-back credits x Scale=regional centers]: retired DDR4/DDR5 packages are desoldered, retested at temperature and re-mounted 32-64 per card behind a CXL controller as a far-memory tier, with the recycler paid by extended-producer-responsibility credits.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers; recapturing ~30% of retired server DRAM as far memory adds an estimated 5-10% effective capacity at ~20-30% of new cost per bit.

title: Anti-weight: DRAM fab financed as regulated 30-year infrastructure asset
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: counter the crushing depreciation weight by financing fab shells and long-life tools through pension/sovereign infrastructure bonds at ~4% over 30 years with a regulated return, leaving only short-life tools on the maker's balance sheet.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost: halving WACC on long-lived assets cuts cost per bit ~15-20%.

title: Harvest stranded VM memory into spot memory capacity
idea: Box[Source=allocated-but-idle VM memory x Transform=hypervisor balloon and telemetry reclaim x Integration=standard DIMMs x Channel=evictable memory-harvest instances]: the hypervisor reclaims memory that VMs reserve but never touch (often ~25%) and resells it as evictable capacity.
why: Raises usable memory by an estimated 15-25% per fleet with no hardware or interface change.

title: Cobalt-free manganese-nitride magnetic cells for refresh-free working memory
idea: Today's MTJs need Co, Ru, Ir and Pt; ferrimagnetic Mn4N has perpendicular anisotropy and low magnetization, and spin-transfer switching current scales with Ms x Hk. Build Mn4N/MgO/FeB tunnel junctions (Mn, N, Mg, O, Fe, B only) with no synthetic antiferromagnet, targeting ~10 ns switching and >1e15 endurance.
why: Refresh and scarce resources: nonvolatile DRAM-class memory on any logic BEOL with no listed elements; risks are TMR ratio and thermal stability at small sizes.

title: BER-certified secondary market prices used memory by error grade
idea: Inverts 'used memory is either good or junk': an exchange tests every returned module, issues a raw-BER certificate (0.001%, 0.1%, 1%), and lists it by grade, so 1%-tolerant controllers set a floor price for even badly aged modules.
why: Reuse supply: turns the whole secondary stream into priced, tradable bits instead of scrap; price discovery raises return rates.

title: Follow-the-sun GB-hour exchange that moves memory-hungry jobs, not memory
idea: Planet-scale, hourly time shift: a spot market prices idle DRAM in GB-hours per datacenter region. Schedulers migrate batch jobs that need lots of memory (ETL, graph analytics, fine-tuning) to regions whose interactive load is at its nightly low, so installed DIMMs stay busy around the clock.
why: Fleet DRAM utilization is often ~40%. Lifting it to ~65% adds ~50% usable supply without any new bits.

title: Certified Fluorine-Free DRAM label funded by green bonds
idea: Combine an independent PFAS-free fab certification (audited chemical inventory, effluent testing) with green-bond financing and EU and automotive buyers who face the EU universal PFAS restriction and pay a 5-10% premium for certified memory.
why: Turns the constraint into a cheaper cost of capital and a price premium, financing new non-incumbent capacity.

title: Nitrogen-sealed DIMM canisters, Project Natick style
idea: Microsoft's undersea data center saw about 1/8 the failure rate in dry nitrogen. A 10-person firm builds hermetic N2-filled memory canisters in the CXL E3.S form factor that exclude humidity, sulfur corrosion and oxygen, roughly doubling module service life.
why: Halves replacement demand at harsh and edge sites; supply through longevity.

title: Ca: CaF2-optic DUV forever-node lines from refurbished scanners
idea: Freeze a DRAM design at an EUV-free 1z-class node with self-aligned quadruple patterning, buy used ArF-immersion scanners on the secondary market and refurbish their CaF2 optics domestically, competing on depreciated capital rather than node.
why: Nodes buy only 10-20% cost/bit while depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; fully depreciated DUV lines win $/bit for capacity tiers.

title: Thin sol-gel synthetic liner so crucibles need 10x less HPQ
idea: Scale jump from bulk to skin: build the crucible body from lower-grade quartz and line only the 1-2 mm surface that touches the melt with synthetic sol-gel silica made from chemical precursors.
why: Spruce Pine supplies >80% of high-purity quartz. Confining high purity to the melt-contact layer cuts HPQ demand per crucible ~10x.

title: Molten-salt electrolysis turns sand directly into polysilicon feedstock
idea: The thermodynamic minimum to reduce SiO2 is ~911 kJ/mol, yet carbothermic arc plus Siemens refining spends several times that. Electro-deoxidize SiO2 pellets in molten CaCl2 (FFC-style, ~850 C) to make silicon directly, then zone-refine, using only Si, O, Ca, Cl and C.
why: Scarce resource and U.S. manufacturability: modular plants break China's ~80% polysilicon share at potentially ~half the energy per kg.

title: Nesting: oxide-TFT memory nested in logic BEOL reusing existing masks
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: a memory layer is nested between two existing logic metal levels, reusing the via mask as the TFT gate contact and metal mask as source/drain, so the only new mask defines the oxide channel island.
why: Capacity: every logic wafer gains a memory layer for buffers, with one mask of added cost.

title: Cu: LME-style physically delivered DRAM futures to finance capacity
idea: Create a standardized, warehouse-receipt DRAM futures contract (16 Gb die-equivalents in bonded vaults) modeled on LME copper and aluminum, so buyers hedge 3-5 years ahead and fabs borrow against forward sales.
why: A 4x price swing deters capex; a hedgeable forward curve lowers cost of capital for new fabs by several points.

title: Blind demand ledger using multiparty computation to kill double-ordering
idea: Worse: every OEM orders 1.5x from every supplier because nobody sees real demand. Flip: buyers submit encrypted orders to a secure multiparty-computation ledger that reveals only aggregate true demand and flags the same need ordered from several suppliers, without exposing any firm's plans.
why: Damps the bullwhip that turns ~10% real demand shifts into multi-x price spikes; existing supply gets allocated to real need.

title: Eliminate the arms-length buyer: OEM cooperative co-owns a DRAM fab
idea: Eliminate the pure-buyer role: automotive, industrial and PC OEMs form a cooperative, like farm co-ops or airline fuel consortia, that owns a mid-size legacy-node DRAM fab and allocates output at cost by equity share.
why: Guarantees allocation in shortages and spreads capex across many balance sheets.

title: Qualify lower-purity gases and chemicals to break supplier chokepoints
idea: Inverts '9N purity everywhere': qualify 6N-7N process gases, wet chemicals and argon/nitrogen substitutes for helium in non-gate steps; trace contamination adds isolated leaky cells, which the 1% budget absorbs.
why: Scarce resource and cost: widens the supplier base beyond a handful of ultra-high-purity producers and cuts materials cost.

title: Halve ultrapure-water rinses in water-scarce fabs, absorbing residue faults
idea: Inverts 'every rinse must be exhaustive': cut UPW rinse time and volume by ~40% on non-gate steps, accepting residue-induced isolated cell faults within the 1% budget.
why: Water and siting: lets fabs in water-stressed U.S. regions such as Arizona expand capacity within existing water permits.

title: Auto-parts core-charge loop for ECU memory remanufacturing
idea: Like alternator cores returned for a deposit, every ECU or ADAS board carries a core charge refunded when the scrapped unit returns; Grade-1 memory die are recovered, rescreened at 125 C, and used in spare-part ECUs that would otherwise force last-time buys of EOL DRAM.
why: Automakers must supply service parts for 10-15 years and hoard EOL DRAM to do so; a remanufacturing loop frees those hoarded bits and supplies long-tail parts.

title: 450 mm died on toolmaker risk: tools paid per wafer pass
idea: The 450 mm transition (G450C) was abandoned around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund development without guaranteed volume. Fix the risk split: toolmakers own and maintain tools inside the fab and are paid per wafer pass with uptime guarantees, so fab capex becomes opex and toolmakers profit from throughput and yield.
why: Capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost; per-pass pricing could cut an entrant's upfront capital ~50-70% and align toolmakers with uptime.

title: Twistor Revival on Magnetic-Tape Coating Lines
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor (magnetic tape wrapped helically on a sense wire) as laminated sheets: surviving data-tape coating lines deposit high-coercivity barium-ferrite stripes on PET film over printed copper sense lines, then laminate crossed drive-line films roll-to-roll at km per hour.
why: Capital intensity: a roll-to-roll web line costs ~$50M versus a $15B fab and reuses the LTO tape industry; yields a non-volatile slow working-memory tier to absorb cold DRAM pages.

title: Eddy-current susceptor pads reflow only memory packages for harvest
idea: Boards carry thin Ni-Fe susceptor layers under DRAM land patterns; a tuned induction coil heats only those sites to reflow in ~5 s. Packages are vacuum-lifted while CPU, passives and laminate stay cool.
why: Fast, selective, low-energy harvest that avoids the thermal damage that ruins packages in whole-board rework.

title: Endosymbiont memory-as-organelle: royalty IP inside every accelerator die
idea: Mitochondria live inside cells but keep their own genome. A memory company licenses a capacitorless on-die memory macro, with its own test and repair firmware, to AI accelerators and SoCs for per-bit royalties, so the bits are made on logic wafers instead of in memory fabs.
why: Memory supply grows with logic capacity, and data-movement energy falls.

title: S: Sulfide self-selecting crosspoint memory without tellurium or arsenic
idea: Build selector-only memory from Ge-S or Si-Ge-S-N sulfide chalcogenides whose polarity-dependent threshold shift stores a bit, stacked as 4F2 crosspoint decks in BEOL; sulfur comes from refinery byproduct.
why: Te/Se/As-free non-volatile crosspoint at ~10-50 ns, density 4F2 divided by deck count.

title: Eliminate external DRAM from low-end devices: MCU redesign service
idea: Eliminate the DRAM chip from products that never needed Linux: a consultancy with an open template library ports low-end routers, thermostats and HMIs from 128-512MB DDR boards to MCU, on-chip SRAM and XIP flash designs; $1M seeds ten conversions.
why: Billions of IoT units carry legacy DDR; removing it frees legacy-node supply for critical uses.

title: No silicon wafer: phone display backplane doubles as standby memory
idea: Forced limit: the memory must ride on an existing non-Si substrate. Low-leakage oxide TFTs already in LTPO phone backplanes get a few hundred MB of gain-cell array in the bezel and backplane, used as frame buffer and standby memory so the LPDDR can sleep.
why: Supply: about 1.5 billion phones a year could each offload 0.25-0.5 GB of LPDDR demand, which frees wafers for servers.

title: Revive deep-trench eDRAM at a U.S. logic fab as merchant chiplets
idea: Mainframe CPUs, extreme users of on-die memory, used deep-trench eDRAM in 14 nm SOI made in New York. Restart that process module to sell merchant DRAM chiplets to AI accelerators, using an existing U.S. logic line and trench-capacitor know-how instead of a dedicated DRAM fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: reuses a paid-for logic fab; trench caps reach 20+ fF without 70:1 pillars (fact 1).

title: Skull-Melting Silicon: Cold-Crucible Czochralski Without Spruce Pine Quartz
idea: Revive the Lebedev Institute's 1970s skull-melting technique (cold-crucible induction melting, used to make cubic zirconia) for silicon crystal growth: a water-cooled segmented copper crucible inductively melts silicon that freezes into its own thin solid-silicon skull, so no high-purity quartz crucible ever touches the melt.
why: Scarce resource: removes the Spruce Pine >80% high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint, lowers oxygen contamination, and turns the crucible into reusable copper.

title: Skull: cold-crucible induction Czochralski growth eliminates quartz crucibles
idea: Random stimulus 'skull' -> a frozen shell of the melt holds the melt. A water-cooled segmented copper cold crucible melts silicon by induction inside its own solid silicon skin, feeding continuous 300 mm CZ pulling with no quartz contact.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine >80% HPQ chokepoint for DRAM wafers; side benefit of low-oxygen wafers that cut leakage defects.

title: Titanium skull-melting: grow silicon ingots with no quartz crucible
idea: Titanium is melted inside a frozen 'skull' of itself in a water-cooled copper crucible. Adapt cold-crucible induction melting, with a frozen silicon shell as the container, to feed a continuous Czochralski puller so the melt never touches quartz. Dope oxygen in through the gas phase.
why: Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint: removes crucibles entirely. Tighter oxygen control may also narrow the retention tail.

title: Quilt: inkjet adaptive interconnect stitches mismatched salvaged die into modules
idea: Random stimulus 'patchwork quilt' -> odd scraps make a blanket. Salvaged die of mixed vendors and sizes are placed roughly on a panel; a camera maps actual positions and inkjet/aerosol-jet prints a custom redistribution layer for every module.
why: No per-design substrate or mask is needed, so heterogeneous salvage DRAM becomes economic at scale; recycle-stream bits up est. 2-3x.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM tiles sold undiced for rack memory
idea: Box[Integration=whole-wafer memory with on-wafer spare routing x Transform=no dicing or packaging x Owner=startup x Scale=rack appliance]: keep the DRAM wafer intact, route around defective dies via redistribution-layer switches, and mount it as a single ~300+ GB memory plane fed by a wafer-edge controller.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by using edge dies and skipping package losses; cuts packaging cost ~15-25% per bit.

title: Supercritical CO2 cleaning slashes fab ultra-pure water demand
idea: Wet cleaning uses water only as solvent and particle carrier; supercritical CO2 (31 C, 74 bar) with alcohol cosolvent has near-zero surface tension, so it rinses high-aspect-ratio capacitor holes without pattern collapse. Replace most post-etch and pre-deposition wet rinses with closed-loop scCO2 recycled at >95%, using only C, O and H.
why: Water/energy and yield: cuts UPW use by >50% at fabs drawing ~10 ML/day and removes stiction-driven collapse of 60-75:1 pillars.

title: Aerospace additive manufacturing for domestic fab tool spare parts
idea: Adapted from GE printing jet-engine fuel nozzles: 3D-print fab consumables and spares in U.S. plants, such as binder-jet SiC focus rings, ceramic showerheads, ESC parts and gas manifolds, qualified tool by tool.
why: Lead times for imported spares and consumables reach 6-12 months in shortages; domestic printing cuts that to days and keeps U.S. tools at higher uptime (U.S. manufacturability, capital efficiency).

title: Ghost kitchen: pure-play DRAM foundry serving fabless memory designers
idea: Random stimulus 'ghost kitchen' -> one kitchen cooks for many brands. A DRAM foundry offers a 1-beta-class cell and capacitor process as a PDK; fabless firms design custom HBM base dies, AI-specific DRAM and niche parts on it, and the foundry aggregates demand to stay full.
why: Unbundles design from capital; brings startup innovation into DRAM like TSMC did for logic; keeps fabs >90% utilized across cycles.

title: Blood-bank cross-matching of DRAM dies to workload retention needs
idea: Adapted from blood typing and cross-matching: each die's retention tail, row-hammer threshold and timing margin are encoded as a 'blood type' in SPD. The memory scheduler cross-matches dies that fail the 64 ms JEDEC retention spec to workloads that rewrite data constantly (KV caches, activations, stream buffers), where natural rewrites stand in for refresh.
why: Recovers dies now scrapped or downbinned (a few % of output) at full value and cuts refresh energy on matched workloads (Facts 3 and 9; cost per bit).

title: Asymmetry: one-mask asymmetric halo implant shrinks access-transistor leakage tail
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: one added implant mask places a halo only on the bitline side of the access transistor, keeping the storage-node junction graded and lowering GIDL, so far fewer dies fail the 13 fA retention tail.
why: Retention yield and refresh (fact 3): more passing dies per wafer and longer refresh intervals.

title: Piggyback idle U.S. silicon-carbide EV fabs for wide-bandgap hot DRAM
idea: Borrowing the EV power-electronics supply chain, run SiC MOS-capacitor DRAM cells in underused 200 mm SiC fabs; SiC's 3.3 eV bandgap makes junction leakage ~10 orders of magnitude lower than Si, so retention at 125 C stays seconds-to-hours and the parts are qualified to 10 years at 125 C.
why: Creates a new, U.S.-made source for automotive/industrial memory that needs near-zero refresh at 125 C, taking those bits off commodity fabs; refresh energy at 125 C falls >100x.

title: Eliminate small-buyer spot premium: purchasing cooperative pools OEM demand
idea: Eliminate spot-market exposure for small OEMs: a ~$500k-funded purchasing co-op aggregates 50-200 small hardware makers' forecasts into contract-size volumes, holds a shared rolling buffer, and allocates by commitment.
why: Small buyers pay spot premiums of 30-100% in shortages; pooling wins contract pricing and allocation.

title: Molybdenum wordlines and contacts mined in Colorado replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Po: tungsten is illegal. Buried wordlines, bitline contacts and periphery plugs switch from W to ALD/CVD molybdenum (lower resistivity at narrow widths, barrier-free on some layers), sourced from U.S. mines such as Climax and Henderson.
why: China supplies ~80% of tungsten while the U.S. is a top molybdenum producer; also trims wordline RC; attacks scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Wafer-form strategic DRAM reserve packaged into whatever is short
idea: Inverts 'stockpiles are finished goods': a national reserve buys known-good DDR5/LPDDR5 wafers during gluts, stores them in nitrogen cabinets, and contracts OSATs to package them into whichever form factor (DIMM, LPDDR, CXL) is scarce during a spike.
why: Price stability and supply: a 2-3 month buffer that damps 4x price swings; wafers are compact, cheap to store, and avoid locking bits into a form factor that may not be the one in shortage.

title: Lost-wax casting: anodic-alumina molds for 200:1 capacitors
idea: Anodize a sputtered aluminum layer above the bitline level so it self-organizes hexagonal nanopores at 40-60 nm pitch with AR >200:1. Coat the pores conformally by ALD with TiN/ZrO2-HfO2/TiN, then dissolve the alumina 'wax' (or keep it as a scaffold), leaving a cast forest of tall capacitors.
why: Capacitor charge wall (needs AR ~115): electrochemistry reaches AR 200+ with no deep-RIE tool, for ~1.5-2x Cs per footprint. An anodization bath and ALD are in any nanofab.

title: 45X-style per-gigabyte domestic DRAM production tax credit
idea: Box[Policy=production tax credit per GB of domestically fabricated DRAM x Finance=transferable credits x Owner=any producer]: pay a declining $/GB credit for U.S.-made DRAM bits, so support follows output instead of one-time capex grants.
why: U.S. manufacturability: closes an estimated 20-40% U.S. cost gap per bit and rewards yield and density.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve: buy in gluts, release in spikes
idea: Nation-scale, decade time shift modeled on the oil reserve: a government agency buys known-good DRAM die and packaged parts when contract prices sit at the bottom of the cycle, stores them unpowered (data retention is irrelevant and the silicon keeps for decades) in dry vaults, and auctions them during price spikes.
why: Damps 4x price swings and buys time to build fabs. A 90-day reserve of U.S. server demand could cap the price spike that a disruption causes.

title: Esaki Diode Revival: Goto-Pair RTD Memory on Phone RF GaAs Fabs
idea: Revive the 1958 Esaki tunnel diode and Goto's tunnel-diode-pair memory as resonant-tunneling-diode bistable cells (two series RTDs plus one HEMT access device) running at 0.3 V, made on the GaAs/InP lines that build smartphone RF front ends in North Carolina, Massachusetts and Oregon.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower via 0.3 V swing and static, refresh-free storage with nW standby; adds memory supply from underused III-V RF fab capacity.

title: Inductive-coupling stacks need no bonds, so memory towers disassemble
idea: Stack DRAM dies with on-chip coil pairs for data (inductive through-chip links) and edge-delivered power, held by a mechanical clamp frame instead of TSVs and hybrid bonds. Failed dies are swapped and stacks reassembled.
why: Removes much of the HBM TSV area tax (~3x area per bit) and makes stacks repairable instead of scrapped.

title: Osteoclast lines: robotic die harvesting and repackaging of retired DRAM
idea: Bone is continuously dissolved by osteoclasts and rebuilt from the same minerals. Automated lines de-solder retired modules, laser-debond packages, retest bare dies at probe level, and re-bond known-good dies onto new substrates as warrantied modules.
why: New-module supply at ~10-20% of the cost of fresh bits, using no wafers, helium or EUV (capital intensity, scarce resources).

title: Vaccine advance market commitment for first manufacturable 3D DRAM
idea: Adapted from Gavi's pneumococcal vaccine AMC: buyers jointly pledge to purchase a set volume (e.g., 2 EB) at a premium price from whichever supplier first ships 3D DRAM that meets density, endurance and 10-100 ns specs. The premium tapers as volume grows.
why: Guarantees a market for the risky first 3D fab and pulls forward the 26+ tier cell (Fact 2), steering private R&D at a density step change (density, cost per bit).

title: EV-battery second-life cascade for retired hyperscaler DIMMs
idea: Borrowing the EV-battery second-life playbook (car pack -> grid storage), retired server DIMMs are run through an automated rig that measures each rank's retention time and row-hammer flip threshold, then re-labelled into tiers (A: production CXL pool, B: cache/scratch, C: read-mostly). An SPD-written 'state of health' field tells the host controller what refresh interval and activation limit to use for that module.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers: hyperscalers retire hundreds of PB of DRAM every 4-5 years; reusing even 30% for 3 more years adds ~5-8% to annual effective bit supply at <20% of new cost per bit.

title: Grade-B DRAM: rebinned decommissioned DIMMs behind CXL expanders
idea: Worse: shred DDR4/DDR5 when servers retire after 4-5 years. Flip: route retired DIMMs through a high-throughput retest line (retention, row-hammer threshold, speed bin) and redeploy them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate old DDR generations to any new host, with ECC strength set by each module's measured bin.
why: Reuse: retired fleet memory is exabyte-scale; redeploying ~30% of it adds roughly 10-15% to annual usable bit supply with no wafers, helium, EUV or fab capital.

title: Bucket-Brigade Analog Storage: 6-Bit Charge Packets Per Cell
idea: Revive the 1969 Philips bucket-brigade device (the analog delay chip in guitar pedals) as multi-level analog charge storage for low-precision AI activations: each capacitor holds one of 64 charge levels, read by a shared successive-approximation ADC per column, built on mature 180-65 nm analog/mixed-signal fabs.
why: Energy and density per useful bit: one charge transfer carries 6 bits (6x fewer cell operations) at small swing (2-3x less than full restore), about 10x lower energy per bit; adds analog-fab capacity to memory supply.
